spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** Rate limiting decouples **incoming demand** from **system capacity** by enforcing an admission budget keyed by `tenant_id`, `api_key`, or `ip:route` before expensive auth or database work runs.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Two-Tier Local Token Bucket + Redis Lua Global Rate Limiter (API Client -> Gateway L1 Bucket -> Redis Lua (L2) -> Origin Service); Local Token-Lease Batching + Async Redis Sync (Client (500k RPS) -> Edge Gateway -> Regional Redis).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Choose the algorithm based on memory per key, burst tolerance, and exactness. To eliminate cross-region RTT and Redis hot-key contention at 500,000 RPS, regional Envoy gateways enforce local in-memory Token Buckets and asynchronously batch-sync quota leases.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore distributed rate limiter architectures, token bucket designs, and retry-storm prevention.

learningJourney.title: What is Rate Limiting
learningJourney.explanation:
Rate limiting decouples **incoming demand** from **system capacity** by enforcing an admission budget keyed by `tenant_id`, `api_key`, or `ip:route` before expensive auth or database work runs.

**Token Bucket** allows controlled bursts up to capacity $B$ while capping sustained rate at $R$ tokens/sec in $O(1)$ memory. **Leaky Bucket** smooths bursts into a constant egress rate. **Sliding Window Counter** eliminates the 2x boundary-burst spike of Fixed Windows in $O(1)$ space.

sectionDiagram.title: Two-Tier Local Token Bucket + Redis Lua Global Rate Limiter

cards.label: 1. Edge Rejection
cards.detail: Reject 429s at the outermost L7 proxy before JWT verification or DB queries.

cards.label: 2. Atomic Lua
cards.detail: Single Redis EVALSHA script reads/refills/decrements tokens and sets PEXPIRE TTL atomically.

cards.label: 3. Fail-Open Fallback
cards.detail: If Redis is unreachable, fall back to the gateway's local in-memory Token Bucket.

sectionDiagram.summary: Hybrid local + Redis Lua rate limiting protects origin pools in <1 ms without a single point of failure.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Rate Limiting (Race Conditions & Boundary Stampedes)
learningJourney.explanation: Without rate limiting, a single buggy retry loop or scraper saturates DB pools and causes 503 outages for all tenants. Implementing it naively introduces two classic bugs: (1) separate Redis `GET` then `INCR` commands create **read-modify-write race conditions** that over-admit concurrent bursts; (2) **Fixed Window Counters** allow 2x quota (1,000 req at `12:00:59` + 1,000 req at `12:01:01`).

ideas.title: Weighted Cost Budgets
ideas.description: Charge `cost = 1` for `GET /items/{id}` and `cost = 25` for `POST /search/export` against the same tenant bucket so heavy routes cannot starve cheap ones.

ideas.title: IETF RateLimit Headers + `429`
ideas.description: Always return `429 Too Many Requests` (never `500`/`503`) with `Retry-After`, `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining`, and `RateLimit-Reset`.

learningJourney.title: How Atomic Token Buckets & Redis Lua are implemented
learningJourney.explanation: Use Redis `TIME` inside Lua scripts (avoiding gateway wall-clock skew), attach `PEXPIRE` TTLs to every key so one-off IPs never leak RAM, and deploy new limits in shadow/dry-run mode (`enforce: false`) before blocking traffic.
learningJourney.markdownContent:
```lua
-- Atomic Redis Token Bucket (KEYS[1]=key, ARGV[1]=cap, ARGV[2]=rate_per_sec, ARGV[3]=cost)
local t = redis.call('TIME')
local now = tonumber(t[1]) + tonumber(t[2]) / 1000000
local data = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(data[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[1])
local last = tonumber(data[2]) or now

tokens = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[1]), tokens + math.max(0, now - last) * tonumber(ARGV[2]))
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= tonumber(ARGV[3]) then
  tokens = tokens - tonumber(ARGV[3])
  allowed = 1
end
redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil((tonumber(ARGV[1]) / tonumber(ARGV[2])) * 1000) + 1000)
return {allowed, math.floor(tokens)}
```

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Token Bucket vs. Sliding Window Log vs. Sliding Window Counter
learningJourney.explanation: Choose the algorithm based on memory per key, burst tolerance, and exactness.

benefits: $O(1)$ memory (2 numbers), allows controlled bursts up to $B$, zero boundary spikes.
costs: Requires atomic Lua script for distributed accuracy.

benefits: $O(1)$ memory and smooths 2x fixed-window boundary spikes via weighted overlap.
costs: Approximate interpolation across the previous window.

benefits: 100% exact to the millisecond with zero boundary approximation.
costs: Stores $O(N)$ timestamps per key—explodes RAM for high-rate tenants.

learningJourney.title: Production example: Multi-Region Gateway with Token-Lease Batching
learningJourney.explanation: To eliminate cross-region RTT and Redis hot-key contention at 500,000 RPS, regional Envoy gateways enforce local in-memory Token Buckets and asynchronously batch-sync quota leases (`INCRBY 50`) with a regional Redis/Valkey shard every 50–100 ms.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why are separate Redis `GET` and `SET`/`INCR` commands unsafe for enforcing API rate limits across concurrent gateway pods?

options.text: Concurrent pods read the same counter value before incrementing, creating a race condition that over-admits bursts
options.feedback: Correct: use an atomic Redis Lua script (`EVALSHA`) so read, refill, check, and decrement execute as one indivisible step.

options.text: Because Redis `GET` flushes to disk synchronously on every read
options.feedback: Redis reads from memory; the bug is the non-atomic read-modify-write race.
`INCR` is atomic for simple counters, but token buckets and TTL initialization require Lua atomicity.

beginner.byteSummary:

_recommendedProblem.title: Design a Distributed Rate Limiter
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Design a distributed rate limiter at the API gateway handling 500,000 req/sec across 10+ stateless API nodes, 10M active identity-policy pairs (~2 GB primary state), enforcing per-user and per-IP quotas across second/minute/hour windows within <= 2 ms p99 overhead and graceful Redis failover.
